# THE CONSTELLATION FIGURES
# 
# This file provides all the information (and more) to work with
# constellation figures -- the lines that connect stars into patterns.
# 
# These figures are the original designs by Alan MacRobert, with
# additions of Microscopium and extention to Telescopium by Martin
# Krzywinski and Paulina Rowicka. The set is complete with figures for
# all 88 constellations.
# 
# ################################################################
# 
# Credits
# 
#   Alan M MacRobert (Sky and Telescope)
#     - original figure designs 
# 
#   Martin Krzywinski (Michael Smith Genome Sciences Center)
#     - fixes to line positions in Sky and Telescope maps (e.g. Cygnus o1-o2)
#     - added Microscopium figure (in consulation with Alan)
#     - extended Telescopium figure (in consulation with Alan)
#     - maintains this file (http://mkweb.bcgsc.ca/constellations)
# 
#   Paulina Rowicka (Harvard)
#     - wishbone design for Microscopium figure
# 
#   Roger Sinnott (Sky and Telescope)
#     - consultation
#     - provided original data file used by S&T software
# 
# ################################################################

# 1 Constellation figures

# 
# 1 -- Constellation Figures
# 
# A constellation figure is a set of pair-wise connections between
# stars, or more generally between any points that may be a star or a
# midpoint between two stars.
# 
# Roger Sinnott from Sky & Telescope writes
# 
#    "The constellation figures on the IAU set of charts came from Sky
#     & Telescope, where they were designed by Alan MacRobert and have
#     been used in the magazine since the early 1990s. They aren't
#     official in any sense, but Alan did give them a lot of careful
#     thought.
# 
# 1.1 - Figures can connect
#     
# A figure for a constellation may connect to one or more neighbouring
# figures. For example, the figures of Puppis, Carina, and Vela
# connect. Consequently, the figure of one constellation can include
# stars in a neighbouring constellation. For example, nu Pupis connects
# to alpha Carina (Canopus).
# 
# 1.2 - Connections may have gaps
# 
# Some connections terminate short of their endpoint -- these gaps
# were intentionally included by Alan in his original designs. The gaps
# are indicated by a flag in the figure records and a unit vector along
# the line is included on either end to help you draw the line short of
# its end.
# 
#    "There are other cases, too, when our lines do not quite connect
#     to stars. For example, in the long serpentine figure of Hydra, we
#     intentionally left short gaps around Alpha and Beta Crateris. That's
#     because those stars officially belong to Crater, rather than Hydra,
#     even though they take part in the geometrical figures of both.
#     
# Roger Sinnott explains this in the context of Orion
# 
#    "Alan did this quite consciously, to give the simple geometric
#     figure a shape more like a man with two legs (i.e., like Orion,
#     the Hunter, in mythology). And as a hunter, Orion has a raised arm
#     (the single line from Alpha Orionis to Mu and the Xi-Nu pair)
#     wielding a heavy club (outlined by Xi-Nu-chi1-chi2). Among the
#     charts there are several other cases of a line going to the rough
#     midpoint of two close stars, because the observer thinks of them
#     as a pair rather than two distinct stars.
# 
# 1.3 - A connection in Carina intersects two connections in Volans
# 
# Connections of figures do not intersect except for the edge case of
# Carina and Volans. The alpha-beta connection of Carina crosses Volans
# and intersects its alpha-beta and alpha-epsilon connections. This is
# usually resolved by introducing a gap in the Carina alpha-beta line
# (https://www.iau.org/static/public/constellations/gif/CAR.gif). This
# gap is not encoded in this file because its position depends on the
# projection.
# 
# Roger Sinnott explains
# 
#    "I forgot to mention one more situation where a gap occurs in the
#     'stick figure' of a constellation, at least as implemented in our S&T
#     software.  We did not want a line belonging to one constellation to
#     cross or intersect a line of another constellation. The best example
#     (maybe the only example) appears on the attached chart of Volans.
# 
#    "In our software, we took care of this and other gaps in lines by
#     adding fictitious stars to the database for the lines to end on. These
#     fictitious stars lie on the great circle between the two real stars
#     that define the line.  This way, a graphic artist who finalizes a
#     chart does not have to remember to insert needed gaps manually.
# 
# 1.4 - Conversation with Alan MacRobert
# 
# I had a great exchange with Alan about the figures. 
# 
# Here, he comments about his design philosophy.
# 
#    "I'm gratified at how the astronomical world has been gravitating to
#     our constellation figures over the years, starting with the IAU. I put
#     a great deal of thought into them. Each is a compromise between four
#     competing priorities:
# 
#    "The lines must include the lines that the eye can't help but
#     naturally see. Two bright stars near each other must be connected
#     because that's what the eye does, no escaping it.
# 
#    "Figures should look like the thing named if reasonably possible. I
#     started with H. A. Rey's groundbreaking figures in his constellation
#     guide 'The Stars, a New Way to See Them' (1952). But Rey committed
#     four sins: He occasionally fudged star positions slightly to make his
#     figures work better. He sometimes used stars too faint for most modern
#     skywatchers to see. He often connected stars with line patterns too
#     complicated for the eye to see easily, while skipping the lines
#     between brighter stars that the eye can't help but see. And, he paid
#     no attention to the constellations' deep heritage in how they have
#     been oriented and depicted since Greco-Roman times. This often makes
#     them conflict with the representations that were the basis of it all
#     and that are seen throught astronomy literature.
# 
#    "I tried to make realistic stick figures that *did* match ancient
#     representations, as recorded in the Almagest star names ('foot,'
#     'knee', 'tail', etc.) and old depictions going back to the Farnese
#     Globe. The Virgo I eventually came up with, for instance, not only
#     matches her ancient arrangement but for the first time, as far as I
#     know, matches her activity: holding the ear of grain Spica in one hand
#     and sowing seeds on the springtime fields with her other hand. I
#     suspect that I rediscovered the original Virgo as seen by farmers and
#     herdsmen outdoors at night before the 'fine arts' took over (starting
#     with the artist hired to paint the constellations on a ceiling in the
#     palace of Philip of Macedon. A king doesn't want grubby shepherds'
#     stick figures, he wants Fine Art to show off. And so it began.)
# 
#    "Similarly, I went with the Hercules who has 'Head of the Giant' as
#     his head star, 'Knee' as his knee star, and 'Club' as the top of his
#     club. This makes Hercules hold out his lion skin in front of him,
#     echoing Orion also waving a club over his head and holding out a lion
#     skin in front of him. I doubt that was a coincidence. And I made sure
#     that Lupus is being stabbed in the throat by Centaurus thrusting a
#     spear.
# 
#    "But a few just had to be what everybody now sees. Cassiopeia is a W
#     no matter what -- even though her stars, including fainter ones
#     connected in the ancient order by name from head to foot, suggest an
#     evocative profile outline of a grieving woman. And Sagittarius is a
#     teapot, even though H. A. Ray's version is more or less historically
#     correct, bow and arrow and all as far as I could tell.
# 
# Here is Alan on my observed discrepancies:
# 
#    "The Cygnus misalignment with the centerpoint between o1 and o2 may
#     have been a slight mistake and should be corrected. Thank you.
# 
#    "Same with the slight misalignments of the line segments that end
#     short of their stars. As I recall, a graphic artist moused each of
#     those line segments back from the center of the star by hand, and the
#     art department was always having trouble in those days of bygone
#     software with good positioning of the ends of lines (they had to do it
#     semi-blind). Look at the leader lines extending from labels on
#     photographs in Sky & Tel from those days and you'll see this.
# 
#    "Line crossing Volans: Can't be helped, leave it as is in the
#     database. You're correct that other map projections would misalign any
#     built-in break.
# 
#    "I love your Microscopium! I did not include any lines for Mic because
#     the stars are faint and I could make no pattern that seemed memorable,
#     much less suggesting anything to do with a microscope. You've done it.
# 
#    "I also like your one-line addition to Telescopium. But it should go
#     to the midpoint between Delta1 and Delta2, since they are so close
#     together and so alike (0.1 mag difference).
# 
# 
# 2 -- Contents of this file
# 
# This file is composed of three kinds of records, indicated by the
# first field of each line.
# 
#   2.1  conpath
#   2.2  conline
#   2.3  conbound_pair 
#   2.4  conbound_path
#   2.5  star
# 
# There is more information in this file than you probably need. I tried
# to anticipate various use cases to help you avoid having to query any
# databases.
# 
# The Yale Bright Star Catalogue
# (http://tdc-www.harvard.edu/catalogs/bsc5.html) is used as the primary
# index of the stars -- this is the HR (Harvard Revised) number. Every
# star that participates in the definition of constellation figures has
# an HR number.
# 
# For completeness, I also provide the Hipparcos and Tycho catalogue
# indexes of these stars, which are available for the vast majority of
# these stars.
# 
# 2.1 (conpath) Figure connection path
# 
# For each constellation a path through its figure is provided on a
# single line identifed by the "conpath" prefix. This part of the file is
# most useful if you're making your own lookups by HR number.
# 
#   conpath And 464(51)-1-335(phi),335(phi)-1-226(nu),226(nu)-1-269(mu),
#               269(mu)-1-337(bet),337(bet)-1-154(pi),154(pi)-1-63/68(tet/sig),
#               63/68(tet/sig)-1-8965(iot),8965(iot)-1-8976(kap),8976(kap)-1-8961(lam),
#               15(alf)-2-165(del),165(del)-1-163(eps),163(eps)-1-215(zet),
#               215(zet)-1-271(eta),337(bet)-2-603(gam1/A),337(bet)-2-165(del),
#               165(del)-1-154(pi),8762(omi)-1-8965(iot)
# 
# The path is a set of comma-delimited connections, each represented by
# a start and end point, which are identified by the corresponding
# star's HR index and its Bayer (or Flamsteed) designation. The
# thickness (which can be 1, 2 or 3) of the connection line is the
# middle digit.
# 
# For example 8976(kap)-1-8961(lam), indicates a thickness=1 (thin line)
# connection between lambda Andromeda and kap Andromeda, whose HR
# indexes are 8976 and 8961, respectively.
# 
#  ***  NOTE: If you access this information from the Sky & Telescope
#  ***  "con123.txt" file, be aware that there the line thickness is
#  ***  encoded differently: 1 = thick, 2 = middle, 3+ = thin.
# 
# In the case where a connection end is a midpoint between two stars,
# both the HR and designation for both stars are /-delimited. For
# example, 63/68(tet/sig)-1-8965(iot) indicates a thin connection to the
# midpoint between theta Andromeda (HR 63) and sigma Andromeda (HR 68).
# 
# Some figures use stars from neighbouring constellations. One example
# is Auriga, where the iota connects to beta Taurus. If a star's
# constellation is not that of the figure, the constellation is given in
# [CON], such as
# 
#    conpath Aur ...,1577(iot)-3-1791(bet)[Tau], ... , 1791(bet)[Tau]-3-2095(tet), ...
# 
# You can also extract this information from the conline records (see below).
# 
# The order of connections in the figure is chosen to create a
# reasonably short path and has no relation to the order of magnitude of
# the stars.
# 
# The conpath lines do not encode gaps. For this, use the conline records (see below).
# 
# 
# 2.2 (conline) Pairwise connections
# 
# On lines prefixed with "conline", a figure's connections are reported
# individually with additional information such as magnitude and
# position of each end point as well as whether the connection has a
# gap. To incorporate the gap encoding requires that I provide you with
# a little more information). The order of connections here is the same
# as in the "con" path described above.
# 
# For example, the 8961(lam)-1-8976(kap) connection in the path for
# Andromeda is provided in more detail like this
# 
#   conline And 1      8976-8961      
#           8976          kap And  4.140  V 
#           355.102115  44.333932  -0.317445   0.948277 0      
#           8961          lam And  3.820  V 
#           354.391012  46.458151   0.317445  -0.948277 0
# 
# where the fields are as follows
# 
#   And       figure constellation
#   1         line thickness
#   8961-8976 HR index pair of connected stars (brighter star first)
# 
# then for the first star
# 
#   8976       HR number
#   kap        Bayer or Flamsteed designation
#   And        constellation
# 
#   4.140      magnitude 
#   V          magnitude band
#   355.102115 RA (deg)
#   44.333932  DEC (deg)
#   -0.317446  uRA, unit vector to other end, RA component
#   0.948276   uDEC,unit vector to other end, DEC component
#   0          end gap?
# 
# followed by the same set of fields for the second star.
# 
#   8961
#   lam
#   And
#   3.820
#   V 
#   354.391012
#   46.458151 
#   0.317445
#   -0.948277
#   0
# 
# When the end of a connection is a midpoint between stars, the
# magnitude and RA/DEC position in the "conline" record is the avearage
# of the two stars (and the band string is now a concatenation of the
# band of each star). HR and designation for both stars are reported 
# and delimited by /. For example,
# 
#   conline Tel 1 6897-6938/6934      
#           6897          alf Tel  3.463  V 
#           276.743402 -45.968458   0.994262   0.106969 0 
#           6938/6934    del2/del1 Tel  4.995 VV 
#           277.973703 -45.836095  -0.994262  -0.106969 0
# 
# indicates that the end of the line is betwen HR 6838 (del2) and HR 6934 (del1).
# 
# The unit vector is the direction of the other end. This is useful for
# when the line has a gap before its end. If the end gap flag is 1, then
# you want to draw the end point of the line at
# 
#   RA'  =  RA + L*uRA
#   DEC' = DEC + L*uDEC
# 
# where L is the distance (in degrees) from the end of the line to the
# star position. The original figure designs by Alan do not strictly
# specify the length of the gap. In the very least, L should be larger
# than the radius R of the star symbol. For example, L = 1.5*R or L =
# 2.0*R works well and you can make the multipler to be a function of
# the thickness of the line (e.g. larger gaps for thicker lines).
# 
# In some cases, such the nu Carina to alpha Puppis
# (https://www.iau.org/static/public/constellations/gif/CAR.gif), you
# may want to override this rule to snap the end of the line exactly to
# the constellation boundary line -- in this case, it's just the right
# distance from alpha Puppis.
# 
# 2.3 (conbound_pair) Constellation boundary lines
# 
# Piece-wise linear constellation boundaries are reported in
# "conbound_pair" lines. These boundaries are taken from
# https://vizier.cds.unistra.fr/viz-bin/VizieR-3?-source=VI/49/bound_18
# 
# For example, the boundaries for Crux are
# 
#   conbound_pair Cru 1 179.070614 -55.695864 179.057196 -64.695870
#   conbound_pair Cru 0 179.057196 -64.695870 194.438279 -64.677043
#   conbound_pair Cru 1 194.438279 -64.677043 194.334403 -55.677180
#   conbound_pair Cru 1 194.334403 -55.677180 179.070614 -55.695864
# 
# where each line reports a boundary line between two (ra,dec)
# points. The fields are
# 
#   Cru        constellation
#   1          duplicate_flag
#   179.070614 ra_start
#   -55.695864 dec_start
#   179.057196 ra_end
#   -64.695870 dec_end
# 
# The duplicate_flag indicates whether this line has already been
# reported in a previous constellation boundary. This will happen
# because each line is a boundary between two constellations. This flag
# helps you to avoid drawing the same line twice.
# 
# For example, this boundary line for Centaurus 
# 
#   conbound_pair Cen 0 179.057196 -64.695870 179.070614 -55.695864
# 
# appears as a boundary line for Crux (now with duplicate_flag=1).
# 
#   conbound_pair Cru 1 179.057196 -64.695870 179.070614 -55.695864
# 
# 
# 2.4 (conbound_path) Constellation boundary lines along great circles
# 
# Each conbound_pair line is followed by a conbound_path line that reports the representation of the line segment along a great circle. This makes for nicer paths on maps using projections such as azimuthal equidistant.
# 
#   conbound_path Cen 0 179.057196,-64.695870 179.057373,-64.605870 179.057549,-64.515870 
#                     ...
#                     179.070409,-55.875864 179.070512,-55.785864 179.070614,-55.695864
# 
# The line is a set of (ra,dec) coordinates along a great circle.
# 
# 
# 2.5 (star) Individual stars in each figure
# 
# More details about each star is found in the "star" lines. 
# 
# These lines list all stars (9,111 stars) in the Yale Bright Star
# Catalogue (BSC), identified by HR index. I've included all BSC stars
# (not just the 762 stars that define constellation figures), in case
# you'd like to create a star chart that included many stars.
# 
#   star  1546016  337   5447  2286-1329-1 
#         And 1   beta bet   Î²  -  43        -
#         Mirach        iau  
#         17.433016  35.620558 
#         V  2.05  M0+IIIa 
#         PM*
#         High_Proper_Motion_Star
# 
# The fields are
# 
#                            1546016  SIMBAD oid record number
#                                337  HR number And  constellation
#                               5447  HIP catalogue index
#                        2286-1329-1  Tycho catalogue index
#                                And  constellation
#                                  1  participates in a constellation figure? (0/1)
#                               beta  Bayer designation (letter)
#                                bet  Bayer designation (letter abbreviation)
#                                  Î²  Bayer designation (Greek character)
#                                  -  Bayer designation (number)
#                                 43  Flamsteed designation
#                                  -  WDS component ID
#                             Mirach  name
#                                iau  name type (IAU, Simbad, supplemental, etc)
#                          17.433016  RA (deg)
#                          35.620558  DEC (deg)
#                                  V  magnitude band 
#                               2.05  magnitude
#                            M0+IIIa  spectral type
#                                PM*  Simbad short object type
#            High_Proper_Motion_Star  Simbad long object type
# 
# All strings 
# 
# The Simbad record for this star is 
# 
#   https://simbad.cds.unistra.fr/simbad/sim-id?Ident=bet+and
# 
# and the ASCII version of the record is at
# 
#   https://simbad.cds.unistra.fr/simbad/sim-id?Ident=beta%20and&output.format=ASCII
# 
# The Bayer and Flamsteed designation is parsed from Simbad's "*" or
# "**" record. The Washington Double Star (WDS) component ID is
# additionally parsed from the WDS identifer
# (https://cds.u-strasbg.fr/cgi-bin/Dic-Simbad?WDS) and all components
# are combined (e.g. Ab Ab -> Aab). If the star has an IAU name then the
# WDS component ID is taken from the IAU list
# (http://www.pas.rochester.edu/~emamajek/WGSN/IAU-CSN.txt).
# 
# The name is represented by a string that most appropriately labels the
# star. In descending order of priority, this is one of: IAU name
# (i.e. if assigned by IAU), SIMBAD NAME field, supplemental name drawn
# from various internet sources, Bayer designation and Flamsteed
# designation. If the star has none of these values, then the name
# string will be the index of one of the catalogues (other than HR, HIP
# or TYC), such as FK5, GCRV, NSV, and so on.
# 
# For IAU names, see https://www.iau.org/public/themes/naming_stars/
# 
# 3 -- Technical Details
# 
# 3.1 - Magnitudes
# 
# Magnitudes were extracted from Simbad's ALLFLUXES table. Where
# available V-band magnitude is shown and, if not available, the
# brightest magnitude band is used. If a star has variable magnitude its
# position in the magnitude-sorted list may not be exact.
# 
# For example, alpha And has a magnitude of 2.06 and is listed by
# Wikipedia as "the brightest star in the constellation of
# Andromeda"(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alpha_Andromedae). However,
# beta And has a listed magnitude of 2.05, which is indicated to vary
# 2.01 to 2.10 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beta_Andromedae).
# 
# In general, expect the reported magnitude of a star to vary slightly
# across sources. Don't be surprised if the Simbad value listed in this
# file is different from what you expect.
# 
# One star dos not have a magnitude listed: tet Ind (HR 8140)
# (http://simbad.u-strasbg.fr/simbad/sim-basic?Ident=HR+8140&submit=SIMBAD+search).
# 
# 3.2 - Star classifications
# 
# Simbad has a large number of object type classifications. These are
# listed at http://vizier.u-strasbg.fr/cgi-bin/OType
# 
# 3.3 - Yale Bright Star Catalogue
# 
# https://vizier.cfa.harvard.edu/viz-bin/VizieR-3?-source=V/50/catalog
#
# version 0.24
# generated on 2023-11-11/16/23 13:35
#
#
